utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the registrar be kind enough to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic, and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours; good morning everybody. Sureta Chana and Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Andres Vatter is the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney diction son, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For today's as hearing, the Chamber bids welcome to all those present, especially representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused and all the staff of this courtroom, and particularly Madam Court Reporter, who is doing a very important job, allowing us to follow what is being said on the basis of the transcript which we see in front of us. I also greet the interpreters. Before we begin with the testimony, I wish to give the floor to the Registrar who wishes to make a statement linked to the transport and travel costs. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Thank you. With your permission, I should like to make a brief statement on behalf of the Registrar with respect to the statement made by Mr. Bourgon during the hearing on the 23rd of June and in connection with the travel of his assistant to Sarajevo. The Registrar considers it important to inform the Chamber, the Trial Chamber, that Mr. Bourgon presented the facts in inexact and incomplete manner. In view of the fact that the statement suggests that the decision of the Registry is unfounded and consequently could be interpreted as calling in question the credibility of the Registrar, the Registrar intends submit to the Trial Chamber in the next few days a detailed memorandum to clarify the facts and to respond to the criticisms made by Mr. Bourgon. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As Mr. Bourgon is not present, we expect that his colleagues will inform him of the position of the Registrar who will send us a memorandum detailing the mentioned problem. At this stage, we will not dwell on the matter any further, and we will move on to the next stage, and that is the hearing of a witness. Madam Usher, will you please go and fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Let me first check that you are hearing in your own language what I am saying. If that is so, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution to testify about events that took place in 1993 in Bosnia. Before asking you to read the solemn declaration, I need to know your identity. So please give me your first and last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vlado Adamovic, born on the 3rd of June, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were you born? In what town or village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a judge of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993, what was your position or occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I was a judge of the district military court in Zenica. So my obligations were to conduct trials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified before in this International Tribunal or in a national court in your own country regarding the events that took place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't apologise. It happens to everyone. It happens to me often. Let me repeat my question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was cautioned about everything except about my mobile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you previously testified in an international court or a national court on events that took place in 1993, or is this the first time that you have been called to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask you to read the solemn declaration given to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me provide some information to you, but as I'm talking to a professional, this information will be reduced in scope. As I have already said, you have been called as a witness for the Prosecution, and within the framework of this testimony, you will be answering questions put to you by a representative of the Prosecution. After that, the Defence counsel for the accused, who are to your left, will also have questions for you as part of the cross-examination. We are applying quite a specific procedure here based on common law, and after the questions of the Defence counsel, the Prosecution may also have some additional questions for you. However, the three Judges who are in front of you may, and this comes from the common law procedure, ask you questions at any time which they may consider necessary in the interest of the truth. However, as a rule, the Judges prefer you to finish answering the questions put to you by the parties before putting their questions to you. After the questions of the Judges, the parties may take the floor again to ask you some additional questions. That would be in very general terms how we will proceed. So as not to surprise you, I wish to tell you straight away that though the nature of questions may be identical, there still may be differences when the Defence ask you questions because, according to the rules, the Defence may put questions to you to check your credibility and also in order to inform the Chamber about the political, military, strategic context and any other matters that they may consider to be useful for their defence. If at times the questions may be complex and long, ask the person putting that question to you to rephrase it. It's quite possible that the person questioning you may be carried away and not realise that a question Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. may cause difficulties for you. So in that case, they will rephrase it. I need to inform you about two other points that I tell all witnesses regardless of who they may be, that by taking the solemn declaration this automatically means that all false testimony is excluded, because false testimony in this Tribunal may be sanctioned quite severely as the maximum penalty may be seven years of imprisonment. The other point is of juridical nature, and that is that our Rules we are governed by envisage that when a witness is answering a question, if the witness feels that by responding to it that reply could be used against him one day, the witness may refuse to answer. This is a well-known principle in Anglo-Saxon law, but also in several continental countries. Should that occur the Chamber has the power to ask the witness opportunity to reply nevertheless, but the Chamber guarantees the witness impunity, and though the words he utters in answer to a question cannot be used against him in the future. This is a bit complicated, but I had to explain it to you. Should you come across any difficulties, please let us know. We are here to help deal with them. According to the schedule, you will be testifying all day. Should that not be long enough, it is quite possible that your testimony may be extended to tomorrow, but I do not wish to prejudice the events. It will all depend on the questions of both parties. So I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for their questions immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has asked you to appear on behalf of the Prosecution in your role as a judge of the district military court, and in light of that I proceed to the testimony of the formation of the court, the rules and duties of the court and the operation generally of the court. So we know that you are a professional, and we know that you are a judge, so I'm not going to go into the details of your qualifications, but could you please indicate to the Trial Chamber when was the district military court established.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I always have difficulty with dates. I'm sometimes wrong with the year, never mind the month. I think it was in 1992, at the end of 1992, by decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which acted, I assume, on behalf of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. A special decision was taken, published in the Official Gazette, a decision to form the court and a decision on the appointment of judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please for the Trial Chamber state the formation of the court, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: This was just before the beginning of the war, when the war was just starting. The need arose for specifying the responsibilities of people wearing uniforms and their criminal offences in relation to civilians, but also civilians who may have committed anything which came under chapter 20 of the former penal code of the SFRY known as military offences, so that there was a discussion as to how such courts should be formed. A group of lawyers advocated that these should be military courts only in as far as they would try people in uniform in the first place, but the laws that were governed by those courts were civilian laws. They didn't differ in any respect from the laws that were complied with by civilian courts. And according to the system of subordination and appeals proceedings, the civilian procedure was observed, because with the formation of district military courts, they had responsibilities for the district, but this did not coincide with the administrative structure of the country in the sense of district administrations so that appeals against rulings of district military courts would be filed with the civilian district court, and after that the case, according to the law and under certain circumstances could be taken up by the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina as the highest-level judicial institution. When I say that the district military courts did not coincide with the administrative division of the country, this meant that the military courts were responsible for a number of municipalities, and I think that the district military court in Zenica was responsible for six or seven municipalities. I don't know exactly how many. And this did not correspond to the official area of the district in the administrative sense. In some cases it may have coincided, but the idea was for district military courts to be organised in large centres or where the -- the authorities who had control in the area could organise them. Once the decision was taken to form those courts - I think this was in the form of a decree; I really don't remember, but there's written evidence about all of this - a military court was set up not only in Zenica but I think also in Sarajevo, Tuzla, or Tesanj. I don't recall now. After that, a decision was taken as to the legislation that would be applied, and then came the decision on the appointment of judges. At first there were four judges. Later on, the number increased. But simultaneously, the military prosecutor's office was organised as courts were, by definition, criminal courts. So the principle applied meant that the courts should act on the basis of reports by prosecutors so that they needed to be formed as well. At first there was just one prosecutor and his deputy, and later the whole office of the prosecution was developed. I think that would be an explanation in brief.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very good history, and I think you answered some of the questions I was about to ask. Could you tell us in which of the courts you sat? Which district did you sit in?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Before being elected to the district military court, from the beginning of my career, in fact I worked throughout my active duty at the municipal court in Zenica as an assistant, then as an associate, and then finally as a judge. And just when I was elected to the district military court, I was also elected to the higher regional court. I think that is what it was called at the time as the name kept changing. And the question was who would be the judges of the district military court. In those days there weren't too many people who would accept such an appointment or who were capable of doing it. And then a rather interesting situation arose. I was meant to start working at a regular court, and the president of this court sent me to the military court, so that I only spent about a month or two at the regular court. But there are written documents about that too. And my career was linked mostly to municipal courts where I worked from 1985 until I was elected to this court. I think it was 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in which district your court sat?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was the Zenica district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the composition of the court that sat in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: At first I think there were four judges sitting in court, Zahid Kovac, Hidajet Halilovic. I don't know who the third judge was at the beginning, and myself. There were three Bosniaks and one Croat. In those days there was every effort to keep an ethnic balance as far as possible. Later on, some other colleagues joined. There was later a Serb judge who joined, Mladen Veseljak as well, and at the end I think there were seven of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber give us an idea of how the court operated. How did you sit? Did you -- all seven judges sat together or did you sit alone or how did you operate?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The legislation provided for the functioning of judges in the procedure since the competencies were prescribed by the law. There were some changes with regard to the previous legislation in terms of the enlargement of the authority of individual judges. When the penalty provided for a crime where -- was up to five Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. years, then there -- there would be individual Judges sitting in the case. If the penalty was higher, then they would -- those crimes would be tried by the so-called smaller councils composed by one professional judge and two lay Judges. If the penalty envisaged by the law was over ten years for the most severe crime, those cases would be tried by the so-called large councils composed of the president of the council who was a professional judge, another professional judge, and three lay Judges. It was by and large the content of the indictment that governed the composition of the council. This was done automatically. This was the professional part of our job. It was well known who would be tried, what based on the law and the internal organisation. The cases would be distributed randomly. The choice of those Judges was random. It was the registry that distributed the cases across the Judges. There could have been some anomalies. Sometimes one judge would have more cases or more severe cases than others, and in that case the -- there was some intervention or a redistribution. Sometimes it would be the Judges themselves who would decide that during their meeting. The president of the court would have a final say in -- in that in order to provide for the equal distribution of cases among all the Judges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you did indicate to us that the court was established by decree. Now, was there a list of offences over which the court had jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was contained in the decision. Whatever I have said so far, I would like to keep a caveat on it, because I'm sure that this must have been this -- prescribed either in the decision or in a separate document. However, I believe that this was contained in the decision on the establishment of the court. Mostly this concerned the military offences that existed in the previous penal code of the former Yugoslavia. At that time, during the former Yugoslavia, these crimes were not provided for by the laws of the former republics. When I say the former republics, I mean that the new states or parts of the former Yugoslavia, from Macedonia to Slovenia. And the so-called federal penal law as it was referred to by the professionals, I believe that Article 20 prescribed and provided for this type of crimes that this court had jurisdiction over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the categories of persons that the court had jurisdiction over? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Those were members of the army and people wearing a uniform, with the only exception being those who were under obligation to join the army and failed to do that, who evaded their military duty and did not wear uniform. However, this court had jurisdiction over them as well. However, over 90 per cent of the cases involved people in uniform, and this was what qualified them to be tried by this court in the most general terms. In the most general terms, this court could be defined as a court for a uniform peace -- people. In Zenica, the need arose for the establishment of such a court, because at that time the state leadership had its session in Zenica, and I remember that somebody invited me to attend one of those meetings. Not formally, it was more of an informal invitation to anybody who would have an idea or who would know how to do that. A certain number of people gathered, mostly from the legal profession, and I remember that at that meeting I put forth my idea according to which the court should be a civilian court, a civilian court of the nature of the regular court, and that the specific nature of this court should lie in the fact that people in uniform would be aware of the fact that there was a special court for them, for the -- a court that would prosecute and try the army. In those days, the main idea was for the army personnel to understand that there was an organisation, both in civilian and in military terms, which would call to task all the perpetrators of crime. I remember at that meeting I was a bitter opponent of the so-called court martials, because I had realised that some of the participants in this meeting did not make a distinction between court martials and the so-called regular military courts as it were. Later on within the army, some rules were adopted, and those rules provided for what is known internationally as court martials and also providing for the responsibility of commanders. In the BiH army, I believe that this not referred to any ranks below the brigade commanders. It could only apply to lower commanders in exceptional circumstances. I believe that this was the case. And those courts, in extraordinary circumstances, could pass decisions even on capital punishment. However, even within that kind of organisation there was some sense, because in the first instance the case had to be referred to the regular military court, and I remember several cases that were heard by our court where the original, drastic measures which were passed by the military units would be overturned, and in some case people were even found not guilty, and it is at that moment that distinction could be made court martials and the so-called regular military courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, would I be correct in saying, then, that according to the regulations which formulated the court, the army had no influence whatsoever over this court? Would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Yes, yes, you're right. The army did not have any influence whatsoever. At first the jurisdiction of the court stems from the decision of the Presidency, and the subordination provided for the responsibility to be taken up to higher civilian courts. And military courts were not part of the military structure. All they had, the word military in their name, unlike the organisation that was in place in the former JNA. For many officers in the former JNA, this was rather confusing. However, we insisted on something that is mutually exclusive. These courts were to be civilian in their nature, in every respect, but the fact that they would be trying military personnel. They were part of the state structure, part of the organisation of the state authority. There was military authorities, administrative authorities, civilian authorities, and there was a line drawn from the Presidency, the body that passed the decision, down to the district military courts on the ground. And in terms of the professional activities of these courts, those were -- the higher instance courts were civilian courts, appellate civilian courts, and at higher -- and this -- at this instance, these courts had nothing whatsoever to do with the military structure save for the fact that they tried people in uniform, military personnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the district military court operated independently of the army?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 325 and 327, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we were to look at Prosecution Exhibit 327 first, Article 2. Does that corroborate what you just said to us?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "District military court shall be independent in the performance of their judicial function and shall render judgements on the basis of the constitution and laws." This is what Article 2 reads, and this is a Decree Law on District Military Courts. I couldn't remember exactly whether it was a law or a decree law, but I can see now it was a decree law which was passed by the Presidency. Here in Article 7, we can see that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go to Article 7, maybe we should look at Article 6.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: "District military courts shall try cases involving criminal offences committed by military personnel and certain criminal offences committed by other persons as stipulated by the present decree law. District military courts shall carry out certain tasks pertaining to the enforcement of criminal sanctions that have been entrusted to them pursuant to the present decree law." And I believe that I've already stated that. Not in so many words. Maybe I have said it in my own words. It's very difficult to remember the exact wording in the law, but I can always give you a general description. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose of the exercise was to verify this is where you get your authority from? This is where your authority derived from, from this decree. And if we look at Exhibit P325, I think it proceeds to tell us the system in which -- the way the court operated, where it received its reports. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The wording used in this decree law is the so-called special military courts. If we go back, when I was talking to the court martials, we could also call them special courts. This word "special" refers to the situations which required for special measures passed by commanders, and I believe that some of the jurisdiction is transferred to the military commanders because of the exceptional circumstances. I believe that court martials cannot act in the situation when there is an immediate threat of war. And this is what is referred to in Article 2 where it says that "the court shall be established by order of the commander of a regiment, brigade, or an officer of a military unit of equivalent or higher rank when they deem that conditions do not exist for conducting criminal proceeding before the competent military court." And the combat situation and security of the military situation required that criminal proceedings be conducted without delay. In order to understand this, you have to imagine a military unit far from a town or any other urbanised area, and you have to imagine that a crime had happened. In order to prosecute a member of that unit, you have to imagine that this would be very difficult because of the extraordinary circumstances which had accumulated and have been described as such in this Article. We are talking about a war situation and a combat situation, and the security of the military unit require an urgency of the proceedings. During a war situation, such courts -- I'm not an expert on military history, so in history such courts were put in place in order to discipline the army, in order to attain the ultimate goal which was general prevention such as has been provided for in the law on courts. In this case, this only applies to the servicemen that may have rebelled against the commander or committed crimes which are against the rules of war, which may have been the abuse of the situation or in which persons in uniforms have committed rapes or other different crimes. In such a situation, the army has to be disciplined, and this is why there was a need to organise such courts, because the final provision here in this article confirms that. It says that a combat situation and security of the military unit require that criminal proceedings be conducted without delay. You can see that it is in -- it is in the interest of the unit that this is done, the unit being the object of protection. And the situation is a combat situation. The object of protection is a unit, and as a result of that, the military -- the court martials were established as an extreme measure. I was very much opposed to using these provisions, because military commanders most often are not very skilled in trying people, especially not in the times of war when a lot of military commanders did not even have the proper military training, let alone any sort of legal training which would enable them to conduct trials and which would enable them to evaluate a situation at hand. We have to respect professionals, and officers who were trained were trained in all aspects of the military profession. However, a war situation calls for other types of knowledge and skills. Those who need to deal with such situations have to have some psychological knowledge. They have to be good leaders. They have to be respected in their midst, and by virtue of their authority they have to be able to deal with such a situation. However, a provision like this provided for only formal protection by virtue of formal authority, although sometimes there was nothing behind the formal authority. The personal authority that was behind that professional authority, if that person was wrong, then there -- this gave room for abuse, and that is why I insisted on being very careful. If such a possibility would be given to people, then -- that this should be at the level of the regiment commander, because I assumed that regiment commanders would indeed be professionals, trade professionals, people who had military training. And some of the military training also assumed that there was some legal training involved in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I asked the question so you can clarify for the Trial Chamber that that provision in no way meant to underestimate the district military court or in no way meant to be a court along with the district military court. That provision was specifically for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to intervene at this stage to remove an ambiguity which, if it is not removed, could complicate the review of this military jurisdiction. I am addressing myself to the witness. You have been shown two documents, one establishing the military Tribunal, and another one creating what you call court-martials. The two texts of the decrees were issued on the same day, but I must check they were not adopt under the same number. The military courts, that is number 1275 of the 13th of August, 1992, whereas the text under P325 carries the number 1278. Judge, the text that the Prosecution has shown you, the decree law on special military courts which you call court martials, and those courts were established by order of a commander, and in Zenica it could only have been the commander of the 3rd Corps. Was this special jurisdiction established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have indicated the distinction between the so-called regular military courts and the so-called special military courts, and it was on purpose that I referred to them as court martials, because in the legal theory, they are better known as court martials, and they're always linked to the army. Everybody who had the rank of a regiment commander or brigade commander could, on the basis of Article 2, establish such a court-martial. I remember that the district military court in Zenica received an appeal or even a whole case - I can't remember any more - from the area of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my question, which is a very precise one. On the basis of Article 2 of this law, did the command of the 3rd Corps establish this jurisdiction? The answer is yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to talk about a case which could serve to draw a conclusion that a special military court had indeed been established. I remember a case that came to the military court which would corroborate the statement of the Prosecution that a special court was not a parallel court or -- this was a subordinated court, and an appeal against a decision of such a special court would be filed with the regular court. I believe there was a case in the area of Breza, and that the sentence in that case was even death penalty. I believe that this was done by a commander. I don't know which court that this commander belonged to, because I don't know who did this area belong to. I know that the case arrived at the military court in Zenica. But this should not confuse you. If the military court in Zenica received a case, this doesn't mean that this case had arrived from the 3rd Corps which existed in the area of Zenica. Why? Because there was a special decision according to which a case could have been transferred to the nearest court which was capable of receiving such a case under the circumstances. So it could have happened that this special, or court-martial could have been established within the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, my question was very specific. It relied solely on the text that I gave you the references of. In the text you have in front of you, in Article 4 it says that the decision establishing this court-martial, as you call it, there is the name and composition of the court, but as opposed to Judges appointed by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Presidency, it is the commander who appoints the Judges and the prosecutor. So my question was whether you, in Zenica, were designated in conformity with Article 4 by the commander of the 3rd Corps or did this special court exist? Did it exist or did it not exist, this special military court? It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have spoken about this case, and this case indicates that the special military court may have been established within a unit in that area, within a brigade or within a regiment, and that a commander did establish a court on behalf of -- I'm now just doing this academic exercise to explain. For example, this commander would say, "On behalf of the 1st Corps, I establish this special court, and I appoint the following commanders as the Judges of this special military court who would try this or that person for this or that crime, because we are unable to reach the regular district court." I remember that there was such a case and that it did arrive at the regular military court, and I know that a commander of a unit had indeed established such a special court. If my memory serves me well, it was in the area of Breza which is some 30 or 40 kilometres away from Sarajevo. I know that the jurisdictions of three corps overlap there of the 2nd, 3rd and the 1st Corps. I know this case may have gone to the military court in Sarajevo or Zenica. And it arrived in Zenica. This case did exist. It must be found in the archives of the court. There may be even -- may have even been more than one. I remember that there were death penalties involved. I was working on that days and I know that I found those people not guilty because the commander in question was nothing but a fool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, Judge, because I think there is some confusion in the debate on the courts. We have a district military court and the decree has been shown to you, and it says that the district military courts are independent and you are a member of that kind of court. You were a member of that kind of court. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There is another decree on special military courts, and you spoke about court-martials, and these deal with disciplinary matters which may at the same time constitute specific criminal offences. And the question is then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The question is then whether these special military courts or court-martials in your terminology have been created, and I think you said yes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In one case that I remember and that I have referred to, and I think there are records to support this, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... mine relates to district military courts of which you were a member, one of them, and the decree 250 relates to special military courts or, to speak in your terminology, court-martials. This is the situation I think. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I see you nodding yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I have got a full answer, but I give you the floor nevertheless. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If there's a technical ability to use a board, I would be glad to draw the structure for you. If there is any technical possibility for me to use a board, a blackboard, I could draw it for you and show it more clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we haven't made provision for that, but we'll be coming back to it, I'm sure. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. President, the witness can put a piece of paper on the ELMO and draw on it. Would you like that, to do it on a piece of paper on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could he be given a white piece of paper, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would not like to interfere in the examination by my learned friend, but perhaps I have greater familiarity with the law in force. We may be able to provide more light during the cross-examination. So if you feel that that would be appropriate, then in the cross-examination I could go into the matter and save us some time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite sure that you would clarify this problem, but nevertheless, the witness can do a very quick sketch for us to show, that, the jurisdiction that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So within this framework of regular civilian courts -- court, there was the Supreme Court at the top. In the middle there were district or higher courts, and at the bottom the municipal courts. That was the civilian courts. In the structure of military courts, this decree, P327, the decree with the force of law on district military courts, related to the organisation of only one type of court, district military courts, and we explained that they tried only military personnel. Appeals from these courts went to the regular court, civilian court, the district civilian court or higher court. And according to the envisaged procedure, they could go on to the Supreme Court. So that was the subordination and connection between the military courts and the civilian courts. That was the situation under regular circumstances. This is the dark side of wartime conditions. Somewhere in the woods outside civilian areas, in extraordinary circumstances, when it is not possible to cross this border because of the distance, because of combat operations, because of inaccessibility of courts, the commanders, the lowest level being brigade commander, can form a special military court or a court-martial, as I called it. He would nominate officers from the army to act as Judges, to be part of a Chamber. They are not the same Judges that were appointed by the Presidency, but are Judges selected by the commander of the brigade, and they pass a decision. And if it is not possible to reach the regular court because of these obstacles, the law prescribes how this decision is carried out. But as soon as there are possibilities for crossing this border, we don't have woods, we don't have excessive distances, we don't have emergency situations, the roads are open, then the case is sent to a regular military court which now reviews the case to see whether the military commanders, as laymen forced to judge on the ground, made a proper decision. That's why these are special courts, extraordinary courts, ad hoc courts. And that is why I put it very roughly that this military commander, who may have been a very good military commander, was a fool when he sentenced this person to death. And he absolutely overdid it. And that is why I was opposed to the formation of such courts, because you need qualified people who know how to act under emergency conditions. When this case is forwarded to a regular military court, again during the process of adjudication, the decision may be appealed and taken to a higher level court. So this line that I draw of -- indicating the emergency situation, enabled the formation of such ad hoc, provisional courts covered by the decree in Exhibit 325, and these are regular courts formed by the Presidency whose cases would be verified by the civilian courts through regular procedure. I really hope that this was of assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, I believe you have assisted us, because I think, and correct me if I'm wrong, that the P325 court, which is the special military court, is only formulated or established when there is an extreme situation. It's not a regular court. Am I right? For the record could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you answer, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could the documents be removed from the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now having covered the formation and the jurisdiction, would you be able now to assist the Trial Chamber as to how the Judges themselves operated? Did you receive complaints? Did you investigate? How did you proceed to run the courts?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The system was fully taken over from the former civilian system that applied in the former Yugoslavia. Without an indictment there could be no trial, and the investigation would be conducted by the investigating judge, which fully corresponded to the traditional French system. The organ for detection was the police. For the military court it could be both the regular police and the military police. So it was quite unimportant who would provide the information in the process of detection. The law enforcement body was the military prosecutor's office -- no. I'm sorry. The body that issued the indictment was the military prosecutor. To make myself quite clear, it was the military prosecutor's office who issued indictments, and the military court would try the case. To prepare an indictment, it was necessary, in most cases, to carry out an investigation. The prosecutor would address the investigating judge with the request to conduct an investigation. The judge would then decide whether there would be an investigation or not, and if an investigation did confirm that there were reasonable grounds to confirm and enough evidence was collected for an indictment, an indictment would be submitted to the court. And then according to the schedule that I mentioned earlier on, this would be assigned either to an individual court or one of the presidents of chambers, be it a small Chamber or a large Chamber, and then the classical continental system of adjudication would be applied. Trials were public. The law did provide for the possibility of excluding the public or closing the proceedings for the public to protect minors or should there be a special interest as provided for by law. Judgements were passed as envisaged by legal procedure. Then there could be appeals as Defence counsel would take an active part in the proceedings regardless of the conditions of war. At least in the Zenica district court, there were no trials without a defence, which meant that human rights were protected, and eventually the higher courts, civilian court therefore, would -- whether it was at the level of a district or a higher level, the Supreme Court, would pass final rulings when they became enforceable. The civilian courts implemented the decisions of the other courts when it came to execution. We would send our rulings for the execution of the judgements to be carried out. What was specific was the involvement of the military police. The civilian courts could engage the civilian police but not the military police. However, we could engage the military police as well, because within the framework of the corps there would be a military police unit, and its duty as to service the court, to provide services to the court. In other words, to carry out decisions of the court in summoning persons, in discovery of persons, or arrest as it is more commonly referred to, although I don't like the term. And the military police would also have the duty, being a police, because that is what they were by definition, to detect perpetrators of criminal offences within the army. Also this was done by the security organs in the army. And this needs some explanation, because their competences overlap. Every police force has the duty of detecting perpetrators and passing on such information to prosecutors' offices. Even if such information were to be forwarded to the court, the court would then forward them to the prosecution, and that is how the circle would function. We didn't have our own police force, but we used the corps police. That police also secured the detention on remand that was used by the district military court. It would bring people to that detention and take them away from detention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, what about the civilians? Were you in position to entertain complaints from ordinary civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military prosecutor's office would receive complaints from whoever may make them. One should make a distinction between the obligation for detection of perpetrators and the person submitting a complaint, or a person would report suspicions that a criminal act had been committed. The police would process this professionally and form a report, a criminal report, that would be sent to the prosecutor's office. However, there were instances of individuals coming to court to report a criminal offence, and then we would send them to the prosecutor's office to receive such complaints, but essentially the procedure would be the same, because then the prosecutor would ask the police to check the thing out posteriori. So it won't be the police who received the report and processed it, but the prosecutor would be the first to receive the information and would ask the prosecutor to check it out. But essentially it ended in the same way, because the prosecutor would verify reported or suspicions of the commission of a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, did the judges of the district military court themselves, did they carry out investigations, specifically going into the field on your own? Were the judges allowed to carry out investigations on their own as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is specifically the duty of investigating judges when they're collecting evidence, having learnt of the commission of a criminal offence. For the evidence to be valid in court, it had to be recorded by the judge in the form of an on-site investigation. So the judge would go out on the scene and make a report on the investigation, recording the evidence that would subsequently be used during the criminal proceedings. By way of an example, in a completely civilian case, there was a traffic accident with several casualties. Several persons were killed. The police informed the investigating judge during working hours. Outside working hours it would be the judge on duty who would have the authority of an investigating judge. He would go to carry out an on-site inspection, collect evidence, take photographs of the scene, make a record of everything found, especially elements that will be decisive for establishing culpability. So this report signed by the judge would be submitted to the prosecutor's office for that office to assess where there are grounds to suspect that a criminal offence had been committed. Now, if the prosecutor finds that no such grounds existed because he -- it is up to him to make the decision, he would not institute proceedings. But if he feels that there are elements, then he would submit a request to the investigating judge to start an investigation. Then the judge would issue a decision on the conduct of an investigation, and he himself would do that investigation pursuant to such a request from the prosecutor. The judge would be bound by the request of the prosecutor and would call the proposed witness, the witnesses proposed by the prosecutor making a record of the evidence, collecting such evidence. But the judge could go a step further. In the interest of the investigation, he could himself call witnesses that he felt could clarify the matter. When His Honour the President at the beginning cautioned me about rights and duties in this Tribunal, I must say that such a procedure has been abandoned in Bosnia and Herzegovina as the one that I've just describe. Our procedure now is identical to what you have, at least according to the explanation the President gave me. We have direct examination, cross-examination, and we have made a combination of the two systems, the Anglo-Saxon and the continental in our regular courts. There's no investigating judge any more, because the investigation is now conducted in Bosnia-Herzegovina by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this may be a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is 10.25. We will have our technical break, and we will resume at five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The examination-in-chief continues. Mrs. Benjamin, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Judge, before the break you highlighted a situation with respect to civilian -- civilian case. Could you please give us an example in the case of -- in the military case, please?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to trials involving military personnel? Is that what you want me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you described for us if -- what happens when a civilian made a complaint to you, and you went into detail telling us what you will do on your own as an investigating judge and whatever. Could you tell us what happened in the case of the military.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure would be more or less the same, the only difference being that the person reporting the crime would be the person bound by a law to investigate and detect perpetrators. In one of the ways provided for by the law, the police would find out that a crime had been committed or that there was a reasonable ground to suspect that such a crime had been committed, and a criminal report would be prepared and forwarded to the prosecutor's office. After that, the prosecutor would take all the action that would be taken in any other case in which there was reasonable grounds to suspect that a crime had been committed. The only difference in the civilian structure and the police in this respect is in terms of the obligation, because the police is duty-bound to detect perpetrators, and the police cannot turn a blind eye to a crime having been committed. And anything that comes from the citizens in the form of a report or a complaint, or anything that comes from the police, that is based on the policework, has to be processed. The degree of necessity to proceed may differ. However, it is absolutely certain that crimes cannot be covered up. They have to be prosecuted. Just by way of example, information that a serious crime has been committed, for example, a murder or a rape or the infliction of grave bodily injury, robbery, or any similar crime has to be processed, and the body that has to process that information is the police and then the police is followed by the prosecutor's office and the final body in that process is a court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Just going back to -- to something that was said earlier on and for clarifications purposes. During your tenure as an investigating judge with the district military court in Zenica in particular, was there ever a situation that you're aware of that the 3rd Corps in that area had to establish a special military court?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say that as I sit here. I don't have -- didn't have access to information about the situation on the ground. I believe it stems from Article 2 of this decree law that various conditions for that have to be met. I have mentioned a case that I remember well. We have received it at the court. This commander had made an assessment and decided that a special military court had to be established. I stick to my previous statement that he had made a serious mistake and that the crime did not call for a death penalty which was redressed later on. However, since a commander in the army did something like that, I would draw a conclusion that it was not only possible to establish special courts but that this was indeed done. Based on the reports that were available to everybody, we can tell that there was fighting all over Bosnia in inaccessible areas. It is very hard to say whether there was such situations that would prevent units from accessing regular military courts, but this again can be concluded based on regular military reports. And if there is anywhere a remark about the inaccessibility of regular courts, be it the civilian courts or the regular military courts, then it is fair to conclude that there was a need for such special military courts to be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. In the life of the district military court and the one in Zenica in particular, was there any time that the court was attached to the military?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I have to explain this, because a simple yes would create a wrong or distorted picture. During a certain period of time, the military court could not exist for logistical reasons. This was during the time when there was no food, water, electricity. There were no bare necessities. There was no paper or other things that are indispensable for the work of any court. And since the military had a priority when it came to supplies and things necessary for defence, the army had at its disposition the available resources no matter what the quantities of these resources were. The Presidency, in order to keep military courts in function, passed a decision to incorporate military courts into the army organisation but only in one of the segments. The army was duty-bound to preserve the existence of the military courts. For example, if we needed paper, we would get it from the army. If we needed electricity, we would get it from the army. If we needed food, it had to be provided. Whatever we -- whatever bare necessities we needed, those were to be provided by the army. However, there was never a decision to subordinate military courts to the military organisation. For example, it was never decided that the corps command should be the command of the court. Such a decision was never made. Courts continued to be independent in their work. The only difference being that we turned to the army to supply us with the bare necessities. We didn't turn to the states because it was impossible. It was the army that supplied us with the things necessary for our work, and they did that based on the request issued by the presidents of the courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this time or this period when the courts were allegedly attached to the military, at no time at all, or can you assist us, at no time at all was the independence of the judiciary compromised in any way?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: There were attempts on the part of some military commanders who did not understand that. And for example, a corps commander, just by way of example, he called a judge in order to ask him what sentence should be pronounced in a certain number of cases in order to step up military discipline. This judge refused to give him advice in a very rush way, and at the end of the day it was the judge who was -- who suffered consequences rather than the military commander. However, not even that attempt to influence the judiciary proved to be successful at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge, could we move on to what I think could be specific examples so that the Court could understand clearly how the district military courts operate, and you indicated to us that there were times when you went out into the fields and did your own investigations. Now, my question is this to you: First, before I go to that, where were you physically located, your geographical location? Where were you located?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Zenica is in Central Bosnia and Herzegovina, some 70 kilometres north of Sarajevo. Zenica is the centre of the Zenica district, a town which had some 120.000 inhabitants before the war. It had a very developed, heavy industry. Since Zenica was the centre of the area, it served as the centre of the court. We had a long tradition of civilian courts in Zenica. There was a civilian district court in Zenica for a number of years before that, and it was only natural that Zenica is the reference point for a number of smaller places around it. Between Doboj and Sarajevo, Zenica is the biggest town. Doboj is further to the north some 60 or 70 kilometres towards the River Sava and further on towards Croatia and Hungary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I get the impression that the court was based in the city, in the town of Zenica. Now, could you tell me -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The very centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What -- how close were you to the Zenica Music School? Was your court anywhere near the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was very near. From the windows of our building, we could see the windows of the music school. The distance between our two buildings was anything between 150 and 300 metres. So we could, from our building, see the music school very clearly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tenure, and I speak particularly during the period of the indictment, January 1993 to February 1994, did you as investigation -- investigating judge at any time receive any complaints from civilians with respect to the Zenica Music School?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, but never in an official form. People would come to inquire about their relatives, and they would come and ask the courts' assistance with the allegations that their relatives had been taken to the music school according to the information that they had. And such reports, as it were, were heard not only by myself but by other judges of the court and -- and then we would refer such people to the military prosecutor's office to make an official record and describe who they were inquiring about and to make it officially known that these people had been taken by members of the BiH Army. Basically we would refer them to the military prosecutor's office to start formal proceedings. It was not just on one occasion. There were several people who came, and we in the court were not unfamiliar with such cases. We were all familiar with -- with this situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a district military judge, your powers appear to be quite wide, and you indicated that there were times -- that's why you were referred to as an investigating judge, that you went out on the field, on the ground. Did you ever - you yourself - investigate or visit the Zenica Music School? Did you ever go there to see what was, you know, happening?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't enter the musical school because the army provided security there. I did show interest in going there on several occasions, but I couldn't do it because one needed to have the army's approval. However, an investigating judge has jurisdiction on any case that had been instituted by the prosecutor. If there is no such case, then an investigating judge does not have any jurisdiction. Even if a murder had taken place in the street and if the investigating judge had seen it, he couldn't do anything. He can only address the prosecutor and ask him to start the procedure. And that is why we would refer people who came to complain to the judges about the music school to the prosecutor, and this is where our authorities ended. When I said that I did want to go and visit the music school, you have to be aware of the fact that we were in war and that everybody tried to assist in dealing with certain situations in order to resolve them. And each and every one of us worked on resolving different situations. For example, a person would come to us and say, "A person has been taken to the musical school a minute or two ago," and then we said, "Okay. Let's go there to see what happened." We would go there, but the army wouldn't let us in. Then we would go to the prosecutor and ask him to do something. Now, what the prosecutor did, the judges could not check because the judges only had jurisdiction over the cases that the prosecutor had initiated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time felt that it was within your powers or your jurisdiction to raise these complaints or to raise these issues, let's say, with the commander of the 3rd Corps at the time? Did you feel that it was, you know, within your jurisdiction and that you should have? And did you ever raise those issues with the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any direct communication with the 3rd Corps Commander. There were no such authorities within the scope of direct subordination or need to shed light on such situations because, first and foremost, it was the military prosecutor who had the duty to shed a light on various situations and the information about the reasonable grounds to suspect that crimes were submitted among the military, and the music school was under the control of the military at that time. I had an opportunity to speak to the corps commander directly. That was Mr. Hadzihasanovic. It was at a meeting, and this meeting was organised by the district authorities with a view to promote cooperation amongst all the bodies that were active in the district in order to prevent these bodies from obstructing each other's work. And I believe that the main problem that we encountered quite a lot of time was lack of coordination between the civilian and military authorities in the same area, and that is why the representatives of all the institutions were asked to attend this meeting which was organised at the International Hotel in Zenica. I remember that the international monitoring mission representatives were present, and these people wore white uniforms. I believe that Ambassador Thebault was in charge at that time, and it was the ambassador and his deputy that co-chaired this meeting together with the president of the district, and I can't remember who it was at the time. And when the court, the military court represented by the president of the court and myself were given the floor, the president explained the need for support to be given to the work of the court, and I was in charge to explain about our professional work and our work on various cases. Then I addressed Mr. Hadzihasanovic directly and warned him about the problem of the music school. I told him that people did come to us to tell us that there was a lot going on in the music school, that people were being taken there and that we had also heard stories about people being beaten in the music school with various wooden bats and other things. And I asked for this to be investigated by the army. And then Mr. Hadzihasanovic told me that he had heard that himself, that he either had investigated the matter or the investigation was under way. And then when I realised that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was aware of the problem, I was satisfied because this was a military facility. And since there was such grave suspicions, I was glad that he was aware of the situation. I -- it was not my intention to investigate what the truth was. My only intention was to point to the problem. The second thing that I pointed out in that conversation was that people came to us very often to complain about their vehicles having been confiscated, especially diesel vehicles. I asked Mr. Hadzihasanovic whether he was aware of the fact that the army had confiscated such a huge number of vehicles, and his answer, I believe, was that the army's entitled to do that because they needed those vehicles. I also told him that I had heard that some units had more vehicles than -- than soldiers. I wanted to dramatise the situation a bit more in order to determine that -- tell him that our limit should be set to this confiscation. My point was that if vehicles had to be confiscated that this should not be done in such a huge excess. Vehicles were needed to transport the wounded or things like that. But if you have information that a unit had 500 soldiers and 600 vehicles in the parking lot, then obviously this is an anomaly. This is something we did not check ourselves because we were not authorised to do that. All we could do was to convey information to the commanders for them to investigate the matter. We received our information from the people who addressed the courts and raised complaints. Some of these cases of confiscation of vehicles were prosecuted by the prosecutor and by the courts, and the final decisions were rendered by the courts and the perpetrators of that crime were punished. This was recorded by the court administration. I don't know whether my conversation with Mr. Hadzihasanovic had any influence on that, but I do sincerely hope that it did. As for the music school, I don't know whether there were any cases that arrived at the court and that had to do with the music school. I only know that on one occasion when I had the opportunity to enter the music school, the same people in white, representatives of the European Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Monitoring Mission, were there. They were looking for a man called Markovic, who was a crime technician in the police in Zenica. His relatives had informed them that he was incarcerated in the music school. Why did they come to ask for our assistance? I don't know. I suppose they wanted the help of the investigating judge. I went with a couple of them. They were allowed to enter the music school, and the same was allowed to me as their accompanying person. I was standing at the entrance to the music school, which is a square building with two or three floors and an attic area with a spiral staircase. I was standing at the very entrance. I did not go to inspect the building. When they returned, they told me that they hadn't found anything in the building. And this visit didn't last more than half an hour. I returned to the courtroom. I did not make any official record of that visit. There was no need for me to make an official record. However, one of them came back to me after a month or so and told me that they had found this Markovic, who was in the music school during the first visit. He was in the attic area. Again, I didn't record anything. This was just information that could have been useful for the prosecutor, and I believe that I actually referred this person to the prosecutor's office on that second occasion. So this would be more or less what I know about the music school and the activities that took place there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Article 7 of the decree law of the district military courts, which was Exhibit P327 that was shown to you awhile ago, gave the court jurisdiction, I believe, to try prisoners of war for offences committed as prisoners of war. Could you indicate to the Trial Chamber if you have ever received cases of this nature, if you have ever tried cases of this nature while you were on the bench as an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: May I see that decree once again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the Prosecution Exhibit 327, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It will be page 4.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I tried looking at but I don't know those things inside because it's only -- only Article, not what's those things. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it would be on the next page, because in English version Article 11 starts on page 3, but the actual clause itself is on page 4. And it starts with: "District military courts shall try prisoners of war ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's Prosecution P327. It's number 11, Article 11.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it. Here it is. Military personnel but may organise other military personnel. I think that there were a couple of cases that came under this Article. I would need to know the contents of the reference to 114, 118, 119. I really can't remember what the contents of those Articles were. Former -- you said "Prisoner of war who had committed a criminal offence as prisoners of war"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the English version reads: "District military courts shall try prisoners of war for criminal offences they have committed as prisoners of war and for crimes against humanity in international law." It's pretty wide.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: So someone would have to enjoy the status of a prisoner of war and to commit a criminal offence as such, as a prisoner of war. We had such a case in the court. I think there was a wounding of a person who had been a prisoner of war but who had committed a criminal offence. He had wounded somebody or something like that. I can't remember exactly, but it could be found.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Then we move on to Article 12, which gave the court jurisdiction under the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. And could you tell us if you, during your tenure, would have received matters of that nature? Would the court have dealt with matters of that nature as far as you know? And the English version says: "District military courts shall adjudicate in all criminal matters involving persons taking part in an armed conflict who are subject to the jurisdiction of the court under the provisions of the Geneva Convention of 12th August 1949 and their additional Protocols." Would you be able to assist us if -- if cases of this nature came before the --

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: This is a general provision reminding the domestic legislation to adjust its system of organisation of courts and their competencies to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. So the laws passed at that time mostly implied taking over former material and procedural laws from the former Yugoslavia, and they were in accordance with the Geneva Conventions with respect to so-called military courts. So the courts taken over were fully in compliance and supported the Geneva Conventions. So the military courts, according to the decree establishing them, had the competence to try military personnel and the rest as envisaged by these articles in regular procedure where human rights are guaranteed, recognition of status of prisoners of war, participation in an enemy army, though who was a criminal offence. So the status of a person depended on the war situation, whether somebody was a civilian or a military man, whether he was a member of a hostile army, which was a criminal offence as such. So the procedure did support the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically in relation to the ABiH, do you recall receiving cases of this nature at all? Do you recall if the court ever had to deal with cases of this nature, specifically in relation to the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The BH army should be seen here as someone providing information. There was a state of war. There were parts of the territory where the exclusive competence was -- or power was in the hands of the army because of combat operations. So where combat operations were ongoing or a situation directly linked to a war situation, the civil organisation ceases to function. It becomes a theatre of war. It becomes something linked to activities in wartime. The court and the prosecutor can never find out what was happening on the ground unless the army itself reports about it. Can you imagine a situation of war operations somewhere in the area between Sarajevo and Zenica, in the hills, where armies are confronted? Who can have any information about things happening there? Only the army or possibly a civilian who happened to be in the area, who managed to flee or who survived the fighting, et cetera. But as opposed to those civilians who might bring some information, the military had within its ranks the military police. It had commands. It had a chain of command. So it was the duty of commanders to report superior commands about any extraordinary developments even during wartime. And it was the duty of the police to process this in a certain way and to pass on such information to the military prosecutor. There were cases which the military prosecutor forwarded to the court, and I learned from that that the military prosecutor must have received information from the army that certain criminal offences had been committed. We, in the court, will never find out whether everything that was committed was actually reported, because there's no way of finding out. Only the army can know that. The army could have organised these special courts or court martials, and then from that file which would reach the military court when the circumstances permitted, that the army had court-martialed somebody or, for instance, they would say during combat operations 50 people were killed. Those 50 people were killed due to combat operations, because the weapons are imprecise and the shells killed some civilians. But it is quite permissible and possible and obligatory should, outside of war operations or during war operations, there were violations of the law and conventions, that is crimes were committed, then such acts would be separately referred to in such a report and forwarded to the military prosecutor for processing, because a war Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. crime cannot be justified by combat operations. Not just war crimes but an ordinary criminal offence. So if there was a killing that occurred within the context of war operations and was not directly linked to the war operations and it was committed by a member of the army, that, too, should have been reported. Shall we say during a battle in a headquarters two officers start quarreling and one of them kills the other. This cannot be justified by war operations. There is grounds to suspect that this was murder that emanated -- that occurred as a result of their dispute. So the important thing was to have a report, and the prosecutor would judge whether such an act should be processed or not, whether proceedings should be instituted or not. We had reports from the army which referred to criminal offences on the front line. There may have been four, five, or even ten judgements of accidental murders or killings during guard duty or cleaning of weapons. Even judges would go out very close to the front line. I remember a location that we went to where the opposing unit was literally 50 metres away from the trench where we were conducting an investigation, because all the troops were on guard in a sense. There was a front line, one army against another. They were in trenches. And an accidental killing occurred. A soldier stepped on his weapon, his rifle. And the commander called us in to record it so that there would be a record of it, and then one day the prosecutor could judge whether that was that criminal offend or not. I know of this case being processed, and I know that this young man was condemned for murder out of negligence, or manslaughter out of negligence. So this information was information that we could receive only from the army and from no other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge, in your practice in Zenica, are you familiar with the term "Mujahedins"?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, tell us, first of all, were the Mujahedins prevalent in the Zenica area?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
