utterances.text: There could be some linguistic imprecision. They were not prevalent in relation to the population but in relation to the army, but that they could frequently be seen in Zenica, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your court, was it ever privy to reports with respect to the Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: There was a case when the commander of the Turkish battalion, within the framework of SFOR, reported to the prosecutor and the court requesting that a judge go and see the barracks where the Mujahedin were temporarily accommodated because shooting could be heard from the barracks. Several vehicles were on fire. Obviously a conflict had occurred amongst the members of the unit. And I remember that one of my colleagues from the court went there, but I don't think that he could do anything because entry would not be allowed to that unit. I think he drew up a report about it. And from the prosecutor, I haven't -- at least I never saw a single case being instituted against a person that you called a Mujahedin. I do not remember us putting on trial any such person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you had to describe the Mujahedins in one word or briefly, how would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: They were described as foreign nationals who had come to assist in the struggle of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the side of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They had a typical specific appearance. They were easily recognisable, as usually on their heads they wore turbans or scarves. They usually wore long beards. They were dressed mostly in military uniforms or partly in military uniforms, and they moved around in smaller or larger groups. Actually, they moved around town as if no one had any power over them. It was awkward, uncomfortable for the citizens to see them. They would drive vehicles without registration plates and so on. Anyway, they were easily recognisable, and everyone could know that they were indeed foreign nationals. And we citizens heard that they had come from various countries with the aim to fight. There were a couple of unpleasant situations linked to them in town because of the religious convictions of the members of those units or that unit, because on a number of -- a couple of occasions in town, let us say that they tried to enforce their own rules. And they would remove young women from the streets, or women who in their view were inappropriately dressed. They would destroy shops or coffee bars serving alcohol, but this somehow came to an end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. And finally, would you say that you were happy with the way the district military court operated? Would you say that you were happy? I mean, were you happy with the prosecutors sending, forwarding cases to you? The way the system operated, were you happy with it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say who, but I think it had to do with the council of Europe or the European Union that once carried out an analysis of the work of military courts, and I think there is a document somewhere to that effect. And the district military court in Zenica was given very high marks. We had various judgements. Some were extremely unpopular in those days from the standpoint of public opinion, and there is no doubt that this court did function like a civilian court and that it acted on all cases that were submitted to us. So the quality of the work of the court cannot be called in question therefore. But the court cannot work unless it is provided with an indictment by the prosecutor or unless the police reports on a perpetrator. I do not know to this day whether the military court in Zenica really did process everything that it should have processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this concludes the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I turn now to the Defence for their questions and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. After some minor technical problems with my papers, I will begin my cross-examination. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Adamovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am Edina Residovic, and we know each other for some time, but for the record let me introduce myself once again. I am representing Enver Hadzihasanovic, and as His Honour the President of the Trial Chamber has already told you, I will have some questions to you relating to your testimony as well as some other questions which may be of significance for the defence of my client. Is it true, Mr. Adamovic, that you were a judge of the Supreme Court at the time when General Enver Hadzihasanovic was handed the indictment, and he gave a statement to you saying that he wanted to come to this court immediately so that you didn't have to engage in the indictment procedure? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: A yes and no answer would not be right. It is true that I was judge of the Supreme Court, but the rest of what you said is not right, and I need to say the following: When I was judge of the Supreme Court, three senior officers were brought in in a manner that I found unacceptable. According to our legislation, there's no such thing as a voluntary surrender. Those persons were taken into custody without them being asked whether they would surrender voluntarily as that doesn't exist according to domestic law. I claimed at the time that through the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina which we could directly apply the Tribunal Statute because from the book published by Zagreb Professor Krapac, I had learned some things about the Tribunal, and I knew that voluntary surrender and admission of guilt is very important when it comes to the determination of sanctions. For this reason, I wanted to give the persons brought in the chance to have equal access to the Tribunal as all the others that are being indicted. And then I informed them of their rights, even though our legislation does not envisage this. And it seems that I was in an absolute minority in the Supreme Court in this respect, and I objected, and I asked that the president authorise one judge. She authorised me, and then I ruled that General Hadzihasanovic, General Alagic, and General Kubura be freed of their cuffs and then they became free men. And he then I asked them, "Do you wish to voluntarily go to the Tribunal? Even though you were brought in, I will order your release; but I want to know what your decision will be," and all three said if they had asked us, we would have reported voluntarily. Then they wrote that down, and I considered this to be voluntary surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have now explained it in detail. I didn't think Their Honours needed such details, but nevertheless, my question led up to the following question, that together with their Defence counsel, you escorted them to the airport as free men; is that right? After that I, as their Defence attorney, and you as the judge, never discussed this case again, did we?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that you were judge of the district military court in Zenica, and is it true that the jurisdiction of the court before the war and during the war and today was always determined by law or by decree with the force of law? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the decree was issued by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in August 1992, whereby it set up district military courts as part of the judicial system of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said, and let me repeat, that in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina in times of war, the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in expanded form, acts as the Assembly which is unable to meet and issues laws and other Assembly acts in the form of decrees with the force of law. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the same composition, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina performs other duties such as appointment of judges and other officials of the republic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: You're reading it, so I suppose it must be correct. It's very difficult for me to follow what you're saying. However, the logic of the matter tells me that this would be correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina which appointed judges of district and higher courts, and it was the Presidency acting as the Assembly that appointed you as a judge of the district court in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher to provide the witness with the Prosecution Exhibits 357 and 3 -- 327 and 325.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I have 327.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then 325, please. Before we look at the law together, would it be correct that in Bosnia Herzegovina, as is the case of the majority of civilised countries in the world, a law is required to establish a court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago we spoke about their jurisdiction and competencies being provided for by the law. You also told us that, but the law also provides for their composition as well as the manner in which these courts will act; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. In this case it was the decree law that provided for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This decree law replaced the law during the war and there was an obligation on the part of the state to adopt and ratify all of these decree laws at the first -- at the first opportunity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I just wanted to be precise for the transcript, because it says here that this is a decree law; that is, a decree with the effect of a law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is beyond dispute that laws are required to establish courts and their competencies. You have told us then that this law provided for the independence of this court which should adjudicate only based on the constitution and laws.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I with like to remind you of some of the provisions of this law. Can you please look at Article 6 of this decree law on military courts. Is it correct that district military courts tried cases involving criminal offences committed by military personnel and certain criminal offences committed by other persons? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that district military courts, in terms of their competencies, differed from regular courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to clarify the situation, one needs to say that regular courts existed throughout the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their competency was based on the seriousness of the crimes that were committed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: You're referring to which courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the regular courts.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basic regular courts were tried in cases where the prescribed punishment was up to ten years and higher courts were competent in the cases of crimes for which the punishment envisaged was over ten years.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Military courts were in charge of all the crimes regardless of the punishment that was envisaged by the law because there was there was no such thing as basic military courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second thing that I wish to clarify with you in terms of our legal system is as follows: Is it true that before the war and during the war, in addition to regular courts which were part of the judiciary system within the scope of the state administration, there are also courts which were called misdemeanour courts and which, as a matter of fact, tried persons who were involved in minor disciplinary offences or minor crimes with regard to those that were tried by other courts? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the district military court was being established according to this decree law dated August 1992, the first court to be established was the court in Zenica. Its competencies should have covered the jurisdiction of the regular court. That means the entire area which would later on be covered by the entire 3rd -- by the 3rd Corps. This was in August 1992. However, because of the size of this area, in November of the same year a new decree law was passed establishing the court in Travnik. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I'm not sure that the administrative division corresponded. That means that I'm not sure whether there was an overlapping between the corps and the courts that were supposed to cover the area of those corps. I believe that there were some areas on the margins of the district which were called free areas. For example, something that should have been under the jurisdiction of Sarajevo was put under the jurisdiction of Zenica. So those things did not fully coincide on the ground. But it was spelled out that, for example, the district 4 for the area of Zenica, Maglaj and Tesanj, I don't want to be mistake in that but you can find it written somewhere, and it's hard to say when this corresponded with the -- with the control of the 3rd or 2nd Corps and whether it corresponded with the administrative division. The competence of this court was envisaged for certain municipalities. Sometimes it corresponded; sometimes it didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question and my -- I may not have been precise in putting it to you, is whether you're aware of the fact that as of the 1st of January 1993 the district military court in Travnik was open for the area that was provided for the law, or by the law?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact, Mr. Adamovic, that during the year 1993 in some places and especially in Travnik, a parallel judicial bodies were established by the bodies of the Croatian council of Herceg-Bosna? For example, in Travnik there was an HVO court which -- whose headquarters were moved in June to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was parallel jurisdiction. I know that they were, they existed, and they were active. I heard that those courts were active, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we were talking about geographical competency of the district court, would you agree with me that west to Zenica the separation of the geographic competence between the district court in Zenica and the district court in Travnik was actually the border between the municipality of Travnik and the municipality of Zenica? Some were behind Ovnak. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I believe that would be the case. I don't know exactly where that border is but I believe that you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on the legal provisions and regulations in the area where you were a judge in the territory of Zenica, there were also regular courts and -- and special misdemeanour courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've already said that military courts tried military personnel irrespective of the envisaged punishment. Would it be true that in the territory where you acted as a judge in addition to the higher instance regular court there are also basic courts in Zenica, in Travnik, in Zavidovici, Kakanj, Visoko, and in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that all these courts existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the OTP, and you have repeated it on your testimony, you said that military courts tried military personnel and civilian courts tried civilians. And this is in a nutshell what can be said about the jurisdiction of these courts.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in a very, very broad outlines that would be correct. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the proceedings before the regular courts was conducting in accordance with the law of the former Yugoslavia which was adopted by Bosnia and Herzegovina and applied as its own law?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what we call the civilian law, which applied to both civilian and military courts to the same extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your military court also applied the penal code which was applied before the regular courts as well, and this penal code consisted of the penal code of the former Yugoslavia which was adopted by Bosnia and Herzegovina and the penal code of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had been in force before the war and during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as judges had a legal possibility which was prescribed by the law to do your job in accordance with the constitution and the laws; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the segment which involved trials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've also told us that there were some minor changes in the Law on Criminal Procedure, and you mentioned the fact that unlike in the past when an indictment could be issued only for the crimes for which the punishment prescribed was up to three years, this changed and that in the war this was increased to five years.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The responsibility of the judges was to a certain extent enlarged, as well as their obligations. More trust was placed in the courts because of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In substantive law, a major change happened in November 1992 when the sanctions were increased for crimes committed during the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Especially this refers to crimes involving property, and the envisaged punishments were stepped up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The town of Sarajevo was encircled and it was very difficult to communicate with the parts of the state in the town. In Zenica, there was a branch of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina which enabled you to speed up appeal procedures against the decisions of your court.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that there was such a branch of the Supreme Court in Tuzla. Those were judges of the district court who had special power to act as Supreme Court judges in a particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about the law on military courts, and you have told us something about the -- the obligations to -- that the army had at the end of 1993 and 1994 to supply us -- to supply you with materiel. Is it true that in keeping with this law the military district court, in administrative sense rather than in the functional sense, at the beginning was -- it was tied with the Ministry of Defence, which is supposed to provide it with materiel? At the end of 1993, it was tied to the Ministry of Justice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were some changes in terms of who would be supplying the courts with the necessities. The essence of the fact was that somebody was always in charge of supplying the court with the essence in order to enable its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you have already told us, between the decisions of your court and the decisions of regular courts, there was no difference because all the appeals against the decisions of your court and the regular courts were filed with the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the appeals court for us was the regular court with civilian judges, and it was the civilian judges, if -- we were also civilian judges, but we were working as military court judges. I want to avoid any confusion in terminology. Those civilian judges were more clever than us, because they were civilian judges and they were higher court -- higher instance court judges, and the intention was for the civilian courts to be superior to military courts. For both those courts, the Supreme Court was the top of the pyramid, the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within the judicial system of Bosnia and Herzegovina, military courts were established together with military prosecutors' offices. Those military prosecutors' offices were not subordinated to army unlike the situation was in the JNA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spoken about that in greater detail. The military prosecutor's office kept the same authorities that were previously provided for by the Law on Criminal Procedure, and those were to instigate criminal proceedings, to issue indictments, and other authorities. Were those the authorities of the military district prosecutor of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: There were -- there was much more than that, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you've told us, there were other authorities, but you have already told us that the military prosecutor was responsible and had its duties in the stage of the elucidation of crimes and the initial instigation of proceedings, and this was done based on the criminal report or on the information that the crime was committed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you've already told us, the military police and the other bodies of the BiH Army were the ones who filed most reports to the prosecutor's office, but those who filed those reports could also be civilians, citizens; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I apologise. We mentioned another context. You have mentioned a number of things, but they were -- there was also information from the court itself. If people turned to the court first, then the court would tell them to go to the prosecutor as the right address to file their complaints with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is also regulated by the law. Is it correct? I can provide you with a copy of the law. In Article 148, it is provided that state bodies, courts, and companies are duty-bound to file such reports and citizens may do so if they wish to do so. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When information was not sufficient for the prosecutor to instigate proceedings, he was duty-bound by the law to collect additional information on the crime and the perpetrator which is regulated by Article 150, paragraph III of this law. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The police is the body in charge of elucidating crimes, and the prosecutor is in charge of collecting information that would corroborate that there is reasonable grounds to suspect that the crime had been committed, which is the grounds to instigate the proceedings and issue an indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will go back to the question that was put to you by my learned friend about the existence of the district military court and special military courts and other judiciary bodies which were dealing with the criminal responsibility of the military personnel. The same rule applies here as in any other court, that the establishment of any court, be it a regular military court or a special military court, which you referred to as a court-martial, or a disciplinary court is always founded in the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This should be the case. It should always stem from law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The law also has to establish the jurisdiction of such courts, of any such court, and the procedure provided for before such courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at Exhibit P325, which will remind us of the basic principles that we as lawyers certainly agree on. In Article 2 that you have already commented upon, and you have told us when these courts are established. According to this Article 2 would it be correct that these are not regular permanent courts but, rather, ad hoc courts which may be established pursuant to the order issued by a brigade commander under conditions provided for by this law?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unlike the district military courts and regular courts which are permanent bodies, these are nothing but ad hoc courts which are established under circumstances provided for by law and for actions provided for by law.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, can we look at Article 3, the bullet points on page 322. There are several bullet points here. Would it be correct that these bullet points actually speak about the actual competencies of this court? That is, they mention the actions or acts committed by servicemen for which a court-martial may be established and for which a commander may order a drastic penalty such as the death penalty. In other words, only these acts are the ones that the court marshall can be competent for; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this court will only adjudicate in the cases of abandoning the line, violations of duty, when it is necessary for the unit to act in order to save the lives of its members or to save the territory. In such cases, the commander could establish such an ad hoc or special court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to say whether this is the case or not, because at the very beginning you mentioned discipline. It is true that we are talking here about disciplinary responsibility, and it is pointed out that the command had to be obeyed in order to -- for the unit to achieve its goal. But there is something here that has nothing to do with discipline. For example, eviction or teaming up with the enemy's side. This constitutes opposition to the unit which is contrary to the activities of this unit. In general terms it can be said that this is done in order to preserve the situation. That is what it is, to give prevalence to the unit that is punishing its member for the disruption of the unity of this unit or putting this unit in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, we will agree that this law expressis verbis as enumerated all those situations that may be adjudicated by this court and its competencies may not be extended to some other acts which are not envisaged by this law.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The regiment commander or the brigade commander referred to in Article 2, in order to organise such a court, must have something like that, but because of everything that is said in bullet point 2 of Article 2, the commander is duty-bound to issue such an order pursuant to a previously obtained consent of his superior commander. For example, a regiment commander says five people have crossed over to the other side. I've managed to capture them. This has a bad influence on the unit. Those are well-known fighters. They might influence other people. I want to establish a court martial. I do not have access to the regular court. I want to punishment -- punish them. And then if his superior is general, he will address the general and ask for his permission to establish the court martial. And if everything is correct in his allegations, then the general will issue such an order. If the general does not agree to the establishment of the court martial, the court martial must not be established. I beg your pardon. I'm professionally deformed, I must say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when we were talking about special military courts, we knew quite clearly that these were quite separate courts which were within the framework of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and whose entire jurisdiction is specified by the law that we are just looking at. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the army, as in civilian life, there are minor offences which are not dealt by by regular courts, regular military courts, if they're not criminal offences, nor are they the type of offences that are dealt with by special military courts, but these minor infractions are dealt by military disciplinary courts.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That relates to the army structure that has to do to the rules of service, the chain of command, et cetera. That is all provided for within the framework of the structure of the army and the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at Prosecution Exhibit 325. Page 333. Articles 44, 45, 46, 47, and onwards. These are provisions of the rules on military discipline which was adopted in accordance with the decree with the force of law on service in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And is it true that these provisions in Article 45 envisaged the formation of military disciplinary courts?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms what I just said. This is a separate book of rules with respect to military discipline, and it applied within the army, and it had to do with the structure of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Article 46, it says that these courts were earlier formed by district defence ministries and later by army corps. So if we wish to round-off the structure of courts that could try military personnel, they would be district military courts for all offences committed by military personnel. Then a special military court, which is an ad hoc court for exceptional circumstances, and a discipline court that was formed within the army for minor infractions of military discipline. It is time for the break perhaps now, so I could continue after the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: If I -- I don't know whether I have any say in the matter, but I would like to have a break, if possible, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 12.30, and we will resume about five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the Defence, let us look at our calculations to see how much more time would you need for your questions, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed one-third of my questions, which means that I would need a total of two hours, and I have spent about 45 minutes of those two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we won't finish today. And the other Defence team, how much time will they need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If we have any questions, we will need only a short period of time, maybe a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Judges will certainly have questions, and you certainly expected it, the hearing will be continued tomorrow, but this could cause a problem with the investigator that -- who has been planned. Perhaps we could begin with the investigator tomorrow and then continue on Monday. Mrs. Benjamin, could you help us?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the investigator is an internal witness. He is here all the time, and we do not anticipate that we have anybody for Monday. So maybe we could finish with the judge and -- so that he can go, and we can do the investigator Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I think that would be a good idea. As the investigator is available, as he is here, there should be no problem in hearing him on Monday. So I give you the floor again, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Adamovic, before the break we were discussing the main jurisdiction of the court of which you were a judge, the district military court. However, the law in many other cases also provides for exceptions. So this law, too, provided for exceptions when the military court does not try military personnel or, rather, when the military court can try civilians. So I should like to ask you to look at Exhibit P327 and Article 9 to begin with. It is page 319 of the decree. Is it true that the law envisages, and this did occur in practice because the courts acted absolutely in line with the law, that when a serviceman and a civilian committed an offence as co-perpetrators or as accessories, then a regular court has the jurisdiction to try the civilian, but that court shall also try the serviceperson as well.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was an exception according to which regular courts would try a military personnel, so that in Zenica during the war, there was situations in addition to district military courts, basic courts would try military men for lighter offences and for more serious offences higher civilian courts when such situations occurred as envisaged by this article?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us look together at Article 7, when the military court, which mainly tries military men, can also try civilians. Is it true that in this Article there's a specific indication of when the military court can try civilians? Let us start from the last paragraph. In this last paragraph, it is indicated when your court could try civilians who had the position of employees in the army and who had committed a criminal offence in the course of their duty. I don't know whether you had any such cases in your practice during the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in Article 7, paragraph one, there is a list of the offences from the law taken over from the SFRY, and I would like to ask the to show the judge this law, for him to look at it, that is to show the witness this book.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wish to ask you, is it true that those were offences under Article 114, which is attack on the constitutional order? Then 118, 119, 121? These were criminal offences jeopardising independence, preventing the struggle against the enemy, service in an enemy army. And then Article 122, assisting the enemy. And then Article 123, undermining military and defensive ability, Article 124, armed rebellion, Article 125, terrorism against a military facility, then sabotage and espionage against a military facility, disclosing a state secret if it was a military secret, then violations of territorial integrity, enemy activities, and all the criminal offences that you yourself referred to under chapter 20 and related directly to the army, dodging service, non-response to mobilisation, calls, et cetera. Are those the criminal offences for which the district military court, if an indictment had been issued, would also try civilians? That is, would the military court also try civilians on these charges?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the court, you probably conducted investigations against a number of persons, a large number of persons, for armed rebellion, and these proceedings were later halted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The court received a request for an investigation to be conducted against persons who were disarmed members of the HVO, and the request was that they be tried for armed rebellion.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As they were not members of the army, having been disarmed, they would have to be considered civilians. And pursuant to this article, you had the authority to put them on trial.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that brings me to the end of questions linked to the competencies of the military court of which you were a judge and pursuant to this decree on the formation of that court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in view of the fact that I would now like to ask the witness several questions which have to do with certain responsibilities of judges in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure and on one occasion you said that it would be a good idea for one of the parties to provide you a translation of the whole law and the Defence has found in the library of this Tribunal a translation of this law, and I would like to give you a copy. As for the other parties, I will provide them only with some of the extracts about which I will be asking this witness. Also, as the Judge has already said, the Judge did not rule only on the basis of the former SFRY but also on the basis of the law of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We also have a translation of that law. So if Your Honours consider that might be of assistance, we are not tendering it into evidence, but we feel it might be of assistance to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Defence could also ask for these documents to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a copy in English for each of the judges, for the Registry, and one for the Prosecution, and only extracts in Bosnian for the other parties in the proceedings and for the witness, because of course I won't be asking him about all the provisions of that law but only a few. At the same time, perhaps it would be a good idea for me to give the judge the whole text of the law, as this is a component part of his everyday activities, and I am sure he will find his way around it quite easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially as he must know this document by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we were taught that we should learn it by heart, but the book itself would always be in the courtroom and we would have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even today our judges, older judges, don't like to see younger judges without holding the book in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Let us not deviate too much from the subject matter at hand. So is it true that this Law on Criminal Procedure was in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina with quite insignificant amendments throughout the war while you were a judge of the district court?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the law that was taken over from the SFRY and was in force. That is the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This law regulates the competences of the Prosecution, the interim affairs bodies, the judges, and defence counsels, so of all the parties in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now discuss what you referred to at one point, that is the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this extract that I have just provided relates to the Law on Criminal Procedure and not to a second section, that is, the criminal law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because I won't have any questions about that law. But I just took advantage of the opportunity to hand to you the translation of that law as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We referred earlier on to the obligations of persons to submit criminal reports, and I would like to ask you to look at the provisions of Article 149, 150, and 151. I'm sorry, 148, 149, 150, and 151. Are these provisions regulating questions as to who files a criminal report and how that criminal report is dealt with?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 151 actually specifies the powers of the internal affairs organs, and as you have already said, the military police and the military security service had the authority before court which regular police forces have in regular courts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the interpreters are asking me whether we have an English translation, but we don't, I'm afraid. I'm sorry. I apologise, Mr. President. I do have my copy of this law, so my legal assistant will carry it to the interpreters in their booth. So is it true, Mr. Adamovic, that organs of internal affairs or security organs and the military police ex officio had to take certain measures to make sure that the perpetrator is found and evidence secured?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that capacity, those organs had the powers to call in certain persons to give them information they were interested in, and without any special procedure, that they could detain those persons up to 24 hours? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those statements which the military or civilian police took from these people could not be used in evidence, and the trial judge could never see them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Exceptionally he could. You remember the rules that said exceptionally some documents could be used from prior proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police or, rather, security organ, be they civilian or military, in accordance with this law, could, if there were suspicions that a certain person had committed a criminal offence, they could take him into custody and hold them in detention up to three days. After that, if they felt that that person should remain in detention, they had to inform the prosecutor and the court and ask that the judge pass a decision determining the duration of the detention.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: This was detention on remand, but later on the detention was counted as a period of serving sentence. So it is police detention, on the basis of police authority, and later on the judge would rule on detention to ensure the presence of the suspect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were any suspicions that some civilians had also committed criminal offences coming under the competence of the military court as envisaged by Article 7, which we saw a moment ago, they could call in civilians to take information from them or to keep them in custody for three days?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they could ask for the assistance of the regular police. I don't know how it came about, but I think it was a positive development that the civilian and the military police would inform each other, and if there were combined perpetrators, civilian and military, the two forces would cooperate and exchange information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are a witness of the practice of assistance, mutual assistance between the civilian and the military police so that they could detect the perpetrators of offences without harming the interests of the public. As you yourself said, this was a positive development, but it would also be quite lawful if the military police and military authorities would take statements from persons that they suspected had committed an offence under Article 7.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I also added what was noted in practice. There was even more mutual coordination than that, of course, when people were sensible and willing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained to my learned friend in some detail the role the judges had in criminal proceedings, and you said that courts would first engage in investigations on the basis of a request of the military prosecutor for a particular person to be investigated for a specific offence, and after that trial proceedings would be instituted once the prosecutor submitted charges to the court, or the indictment; is that right? However, is it also correct -- can you look at Article 156 in the penal code to remind ourselves. Is it true that the laws regulated such situations in which the investigating judge, upon receiving information that a crime had been committed and this information he could receive primarily from the military police or from anybody else for that matter, such a judge could carry out some investigation even before the prosecutor officially requested for the investigation to be carried out?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The way you worded your question is before the Prosecution asks for the investigation. In Article 156 it refers to the activities of the investigating judge who has the actual competency to examine the request of the prosecutor as well as of the judge who is not actually competent but is rather a lower instance court judge who by virtue of the matter could not try such a case let alone be investigative judge. So such a judge can carry out certain actions in order to obtain evidence which could not be otherwise obtained because of the delay. And this is what it says here. These actions whose postponement would be risky even before a decision to conduct an inquiry, but the competent public prosecutor must be informed of everything that is done. Evidence has to be provided, and this exception relates to that particular situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is exactly what I was going to ask you. These are the cases that you explained about in response to my learned friend's question. For example, there is a fire, a murder, or burglary, and in order for evidence to be obtained, an investigative judge is sent to the spot and take action which are provided for in the law; is that correct? As a rule, the competent prosecution had to be present as well as the military or civilian police. However, irrespective of that, the judge was duty-bound to inform the military prosecution of all the actions that he had undertaken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to bear in mind that the judges were not the ones to instigate procedures. They could obtain evidence, because the one who instigates proceedings cannot guarantee the validity of evidence. Before the trial to provide for the validity, the judge was sent to the spot to obtain evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, irrespective of the fact that you as a judge would forward the record and the evidence to the prosecutor, the court has kept a copy of that record and a KRI number was given to such record?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a paper trail that corroborated what the judges have done, and this was also a way to control the processing of such a case. For example, if the aggrieved party in this case is in a position to re-examine the -- the previous case and its existence, and if it is discovered that this case has been misplaced or misused by the prosecutor, such an aggrieved party had always at his disposal the archives of the court to verify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During an on-site investigation, if the judge found on the spot the eyewitnesses of the event, the judge would take their statements, their brief statements. The judge would also record their personal data so as to enable the prosecutor to access these witnesses in the future.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're referring to Article 156. As a matter of fact, it is Article 238 where it says that the on-site inspection is carried out when the immediate knowledge is necessary. From this it stems that in order to provide the evidence for the court, the investigating judge has to be sent to the spot. In Article 156, this authority is also given to the judges who do not have competencies and the ultimate goal is to obtain evidence in order to instigate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would also obtain information about eye witnesses. You would record that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was even a possibility provided to us to carry out interviews, because here also the postponement or delay was dangerous. For example, somebody may have been injured, and the injury may have been lethal. So this person had to be interviewed immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems that we are too fast. On the spot of the crime, the judge could also order somebody to be remanded in custody if the suspect was found on the spot.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by the police on the request of the authorised judge who had grounds to believe that a crime was committed. However, the authorities of the judge in remanding somebody in custody was relative to the time given to the prosecutor to instigate proceedings. In general terms, one may say that the judge may have ordered somebody to be remanded in custody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, the judge could also issue an order to other bodies to carry out certain investigative actions. For example, exhumation, paraffin glove expertise or any other investigative procedure leading to obtaining evidence for a future procedure?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: These special investigative procedures which are specified in the new law on are not similar to the ones that were provided for before are relative to the on-site inspection. The requirement to carry out an on-site inspection call for the activity of the judge. The things that you have now mentioned are part of the regular procedure, subsequent procedure. However, if a perpetrator or a suspect was found on the spot with a pistol in his hand, every judge would order for this person to be subject to a paraffin glove test in order to see whether there are any traces of gunpowder on the hand of the person. You have to know that such traces remain on the skin for only a limited period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that a judge was on the spot and in 99 per cent the prosecutor as well, and it is the judge that's admitted the complete documentation to the prosecutor, everything else that happened in the proceedings was carried out on the order of the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the prior court's approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now a few questions about problems in detection, prosecution, and adjudication. You were telling us about very hard conditions of your work. You didn't have paper or any other resources. In general terms, could you maybe confirm that during 1993 and 1994, all the bodies and law enforcement agencies in Zenica faced huge problems which made the performance of your duties extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: War always brings extreme conditions, and all the bodies worked in extreme conditions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the problem of resources, you as a judge faced another major problem, and that was a huge number of refugees and a major fluctuation of people in the area. So it was very difficult for you to establish the identity and the place of residence for -- of certain suspects or witnesses to your future case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was just one of the problems that we faced in the processing of war crimes and crimes in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, as you have already told us, the problems arose from the war situation itself, because not far from Zenica combat operations were taking place, and there were front lines in the vicinity, especially during 1993, facing the Army of Republika Srpska and the Croatian Defence Council; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also faced the fact that a number of crimes were perpetrated during the night by unknown perpetrators. Very often the military police and the security organs complained about extremely -- extremely huge problems in obtaining evidence as to who was it who perpetrated certain crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: There's no rule about when crimes are committed. They can be committed in the morning, in the afternoon, or during the night. The general complaint was that the conditions of work are aggravated by the war situation. Everything that is normal in peacetime and that can be done very fast in peacetime starting with establishing communication, transportation to the spot of the crime in the wartime is slowed down or totally impossible because of the conditions of war. However, it would also happen that we would be informed that something was absolutely impossible and then we would go to the police and find the police officers playing cards. And then their commander would order them to go somewhere. Sometimes they just couldn't be bothered. They didn't want to go to the spot of crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, in your role as a judge you encountered situations when people would carry arms illegally. There were people who also wore uniforms, and they were not members of the army. There was also false identification by persons who wanted to enter other people's apartments; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had such things in our judicial practice. However, in everyday life, we have to bear in mind who was it who was in charge of that. The given place dealt quite successfully with such cases. However, everybody who wore a uniform would also carry arms. Who was it who checked who these people were? We couldn't know it. I can just tell you that when you came across a person in uniform carrying arms, an average person would immediately think that that person was a soldier. And it was only the army or the army police, the military police, who could check that. It was very difficult to spot a civilian with the arms, and the civilian police would react immediately. The information that you have just mentioned is the information that can be found in the court documents. People would inform us about people who carried illegal weapons and were not soldiers, people who falsely impersonated people and said they were who they were not to break into people's apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Adamovic, that the investigations were encumbered with, and that is the fact that a significant number of people, especially from the vicinity of Zenica and Zenica itself would go to the areas under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, and these areas were banned to the military police, the military prosecutors, or you as judges, so none of you could go there and carry out your investigations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: The crime can cross all the borders, even during the war. It has always been the case in every country in the world. Now, one would have to analyse to what extent this happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were cases of people fleeing to the enemy territory, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very often it was sometimes impossible to carry out an interview with the victims, because those people would also leave to the areas that were under the control of the HVO, and you as a judge did not have the means to summon them and to hear them before the -- before the court at that time.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I answered that, then I would have to quote some of my cases. I don't remember in any of my cases that I was unable to hear people. There was always a possibility for you to look for somebody who had crossed to the other side. But this applied less to the victims and more to the criminals, irrespective of their ethnic background. Those criminals would flee to the territory where they were sure they would not be arrested. There were a few places the on the border where criminals could always cross the border and do their business. A normal citizen would not be able to do that. They were not in a position to do that. And these were the places where the largest abuse of uniform and weapons took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Adamovic, that the military police, although it did have information that something had taken place, sometimes could not get hold of enough evidence or enough information that this was indeed a crime rather than an accident, and that in such a situation the military police did not have enough grounds to file a criminal report. In that case, they would hold on to the file until the moment they have more evidence, enough evidence for submission of that report to the prosecutor. Was that the situation in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the military police did in those -- in that respect. I didn't cooperate with the military police in that respect. I know that every time a judge was called to the site after a certain time the judge would ask to see what was done in respect of the orders that stemmed from their on-site investigation. And in one way or another, we kept control or finalised our work. In cases, as the one that you have mentioned, it is very possible that a certain number of cases or files were encumbered with the difficulty in obtaining evidence due to the accumulated degree which would be sufficient for a criminal report. However, the relationship with the prosecutor and the police should have been such so as to not extend that beyond any deadlines. The prosecutor also had to have and exert some control and check why some cases were stalled. If this hadn't been done, this would open room for abuse, because, for example, imagine a situation where a prosecutor called the military police to ask what was going on the military police says, "Well, we haven't got enough evidence." If that was indeed the case, then the -- an order should be -- should have been given for -- for other means to be employed to obtain evidence. If the police, on the other hand, for example, said to the prosecution, "We went to the ground. We didn't find anybody," then this was abuse of position. In some cases you did file a criminal report against the military police for abuse of their position in the army, and this was recorded. We did that because we had noticed that the members of the army actually sabotaged our work or provided us with false information, or we did that in order to preserve the authority of the court in a crisis situation. We wanted to so them that they couldn't behave in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pauses between questions and answers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to finish what I was saying. Everything was possible. Everything was prescribed by law. All the services existed, and I'm claiming seriously that everything depended on how much people were ready to do, whether they were tricking or cheating each other, whether they were serious or not. There was the system. There was the police to detect. There was the prosecutor to prosecute. There was the court to try. Whether any of these segments should have acted properly and did not do so can be seen in the various stages of the proceedings. You enter the court. You look at the files. All have been recorded, and you see for which no judgements were made. In the case of the prosecutor, one has to see whether all the criminal reports he received he passed on to the court in the form of a request for an investigation or by issuing an indictment, or did he close the case feeling that there was no grounds for continuing the proceedings. Again there must be a record of this. Then there's also the police. One has to look at the complaints of citizens and things that are public knowledge, whether this has been recorded in the police. And then you will see what each of these segments did and what they didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your lengthy answer. I'm sure he know, like I do, that there is a figure of crime, that is the crime rate.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm not talking about that. I'm talking about to what extent each entity worked seriously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under wartime conditions, this crime rate is greater, and it is more difficult to get hold of data than in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: VLADO ADAMOVIC
utterances.text: It was to be expected that the crime rate should go up drastically because of wartime conditions, but strangely enough, and I was explaining this at a professional rally, the crime rate did not increase in Bosnia and Herzegovina to the extent expected. I don't know what the explanation is, but it does not correspond to similar figures in other countries at war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move on to another matter. I'll be coming back to this question later using some figures, but is it true, Mr. Adamovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am looking at the clock, and we will continue tomorrow. So, Judge Adamovic, you must not have any contact with anyone from now until tomorrow. You are a witness of the court now. You don't belong to any party. So please be back here tomorrow for the hearing, which will begin at 9.00 a.m. And I think that during the day we will finish your testimony by 13.45 at the latest. If there is no other matter on the agenda, the hearing is adjourned, and I invite you all to be back here tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. I shall give back to the registrar two exhibits that he gave me which have been registered, and I wish to return them to him. Thank you.
